paper_title: Algorithms for the self-optimisation of chemical reactions
mechanistic_insights: Local optimization algorithms (e.g., Nelder-Mead simplex, steepest descent) are fast but may converge on a local optimum, making them suitable for systems assumed to have a single optimum.
Global optimization algorithms (e.g., SNOBFIT) are more robust for noisy systems or complex response surfaces with multiple optima, as they balance exploration and exploitation.
Bayesian optimization uses a surrogate model (e.g., Gaussian Process) and an acquisition function to efficiently suggest new experiments, making it ideal for expensive-to-evaluate chemical systems.
Multi-objective optimization algorithms (e.g., TSEMO) are required when optimizing for conflicting objectives (e.g., yield vs. cost), generating a Pareto front of optimal trade-off solutions.
Most documented self-optimization algorithms struggle with a combination of discrete (e.g., solvent, catalyst) and continuous variables, representing an area for future development.

quantitative_outcomes.notes: This is a review paper on algorithms for the self-optimization of chemical reactions. It does not present primary experimental data for a specific reaction but discusses various algorithmic approaches (local, global, multi-objective) and cites their application in optimizing different chemical systems from prior literature.
